title: September minutes connect a fourth rate rise to services inflation, AI investment and the real yield curve
summary: The Monetary Policy Board voted unanimously on 29 September to raise the cash rate from 4.35% to 4.60%. The 28–29 September minutes were published on 13 October. In August the Board had held while awaiting evidence on three upside risks. By September, the Middle East conflict had escalated, demand for inputs used in AI was contributing to broader cost pressures, and the latest Australian price and activity data suggested domestic capacity was tighter than assumed. The members accepted that the combination worsened the short-term trade-off for employment. Their judgement was that delaying action would make a timely return to target less likely (Economic conditions and Considerations for monetary policy).

July inflation exceeded the August projection, especially in market services. Petrol and diesel prices were around 13% above the levels staff had expected, and the share of items rising faster than 2.5% was well above average. Staff’s preliminary breakdown suggested the surprise in underlying inflation reflected greater domestic capacity pressure more than unexpectedly rapid pass-through of the Middle East energy shock. This attribution matters. Petrol prices could fall back if shipping normalised, while broad services pressure and sustained unit labour costs would remain even after that improvement. Monthly price data are noisy and liaison reports of broad cost increases supplied corroborating evidence, not an independent measurement of the output gap (Economic conditions).

AI demand entered through trade, physical inputs and investment. Australia’s Asian trading partners had again grown faster than forecast. Prices of constrained technology components were rising and some Australian firms reported higher software and IT costs. Domestic private business investment rose more than 10% over the year to the June quarter, with significant data-centre and renewable-energy construction as well as strength elsewhere. By comparison, household consumption growth was below trend and established housing prices were falling faster than expected. The Board noted that consumption might need to grow slowly while other expenditures claimed a large share of the economy’s limited capacity. Strong aggregate demand therefore did not imply strong conditions for every consumer-facing firm (Economic conditions).

Unemployment had risen to 4.6% in August alongside higher participation. The Board cautioned about changes in labour-force survey methodology. Most forward-looking demand indicators implied stability, with some job advertisements firmer. Staff began to question whether the unemployment rate compatible with the inflation target might be higher than assumed in August. With weak productivity, unit labour costs could stay elevated even if wage growth was less striking. A higher measured unemployment rate therefore did not conclusively demonstrate sufficient slack. Conversely, falling housing activity and further lagged effects of previous increases might reduce demand by more than forecast. The Board considered these possibilities when weighing a hold (Economic conditions and Considerations for monetary policy).

The discussion of bond yields is critical to interpreting the degree of restraint. Longer-dated government yields had risen across advanced economies and the increase appeared concentrated in real yields. Longer-term inflation compensation remained broadly consistent with targets. A higher equilibrium real rate would make a given cash rate less restrictive. A higher term premium would instead raise the cost of long borrowing for a given path of short rates. More debt issuance, changes in the investor base and greater uncertainty could contribute to the latter. Neither component is directly observed. In Australia the effect of the term premium on households might be relatively modest because borrowing costs commonly reference the short end. Large moves in long gilts or Treasuries therefore need not deliver the same volume of Australian mortgage restraint (Financial conditions).

Other assets and credit quantities reinforced the mixed picture. Australian shares had fallen around 5% since the last meeting, with weaker expected earnings in banks, real estate and discretionary consumption. Corporate funding nevertheless remained readily available and business credit growth was strong. The real trade-weighted Australian dollar was somewhat above the range of estimated longer-run equilibrium values and might be adding a little restraint. Scheduled mortgage payments stood near 10% of household disposable income, around the prior peak, while extra repayments were a little below average. Relative overseas tightening could weaken the currency at an unchanged Australian cash rate, adding another channel through which global rates might matter. Markets and all surveyed economists expected an increase at this decision, so the quarter point alone would be a poor proxy for surprise (Financial conditions).

The separate financial stability assessment exposed an important distributional difference. For the median mortgagor in the lowest income quintile, buffers were just under one year of scheduled repayments. The equivalent in the highest quintile was almost two years. Few borrowers had negative equity, and staff analysis still found few under a hypothetical 20% house-price fall. Some mortgagors were nevertheless curtailing discretionary spending. Low-income renters could face greater stress from inflation without the housing equity or cash balances of typical mortgage borrowers. Capital resilience to credit losses thus did not mean a rate rise had small effects on consumption or welfare. Foreign sovereign markets and highly valued, increasingly indebted AI firms were potential sources of a broader repricing (Financial stability assessment).

The external risk assessment also separated the prospects of a technology from the valuation of the firms financing it. Capital expenditure brought rising debt and, in some cases, less transparent commitments. Strong earnings had so far contained leverage, yet market prices required sustained profit growth that might disappoint even if the technology succeeded. Funds facing a sudden demand for cash would have to manage liquidity, a point the Board raised in relation to Australian superannuation portfolios (Financial stability assessment).

Members judged that a 25 basis point increase offered protection against a drawn-out inflation overshoot and a possible increase in firms’ medium-term expectations. The earlier projection depended on productivity recovering, demand growing below supply and expectations staying stable. Several of these conditions were now less secure. Members weighed stronger-than-assumed housing effects, lagged rate transmission and a larger demand shock from the conflict. In the near term, business investment, leading labour indicators and private buffers reduced their concern about a sharp contraction. All nine ultimately favoured tightening while retaining their employment objective. The minutes separately endorse future regular auctions of longer-term repo funding, envisaged to become operational in 2027. This was a decision about liquidity operations, with no evidence in the minutes of contemporaneous emergency lending or a reversal of the cash-rate action (Considerations for monetary policy, The decision and Liquidity operations).

questions.question: Did the July inflation surprise reflect domestic capacity rather than cost pass-through?
questions.detail: Decompose original-release price changes into labour-intensive services, energy-intensive goods and items exposed to imported technology costs. Combine those readings with contemporaneous capacity surveys, unit labour costs and firms’ pricing reports. Separate forecast errors from inflation levels. Persistent upward surprises among low-energy domestic services would support the staff explanation more directly than a higher headline reading driven by motor fuel.

questions.question: How much did the higher real yield represent equilibrium rates rather than a term premium?
questions.detail: Compare traded real yields with survey expectations for future short rates and alternative term-structure estimates. Check how each interpretation predicts actual bank funding, corporate spreads and mortgage rates, where maturities differ. Global issuance and AI financing can affect both equilibrium rates and term premia. A model allocation is sensitive to assumptions, so include measures of uncertainty and contemporaneous Australian-dollar movements.

questions.question: Whose spending responded most to higher rates when aggregate mortgage buffers remained large?
questions.detail: Follow low-buffer and high-buffer mortgagors, debt-free owners and low-income renters separately. Match on income shocks, regional housing turnover and fuel exposure. Test whether weakening discretionary spending preceded missed payments. Household resilience in a negative-equity stress test can coexist with substantial consumption restraint, particularly for groups that scarcely feature in a mortgage-arrears dataset.
